title: Git Fundamentals
tagline: Three areas, one command pattern -- every other Git command is a variation on moving files between them.

concept.label: What
concept.text: A version-control system tracking snapshots of a project over time, stored in a hidden .git folder.

concept.label: Why
concept.text: Without it, "final_v2_REALLY_final.docx" is your version history -- Git replaces that with real, queryable history.

concept.label: How
concept.text: Three areas: working directory (your files) -> staging area (git add) -> repository (git commit).

concept.label: When
concept.text: The moment a project has more than one file you'd be sad to lose -- which is almost immediately.

concept.label: Where
concept.text: Every chapter after this one is built on these three areas and two commands.

mnemonic.label: W.S.R.
mnemonic.text: Working directory -> Staging -> Repository -- the one-way path every change takes

sandboxNote.text: these are real commands for a terminal with git installed -- type them into an actual shell (or GitHub Codespaces / Replit) to see real output, not this page.

code:
git init                        # create a new repo (a .git folder) here
git status                      # ALWAYS run this first -- shows what's changed

echo "hello" > notes.txt        # a change in the WORKING DIRECTORY
git add notes.txt               # move it to the STAGING AREA
git status                      # notice it's now "staged", not just "modified"

git commit -m "Add notes.txt"   # move staged changes into the REPOSITORY
git log                         # see the permanent snapshot you just created

cycle.title: Read the concept table once
cycle.text: Don't memorise commands yet. Just notice the pattern: What it is -> Why it matters -> How the three areas connect -> When -> Where.

cycle.title: Type the code yourself — no copy-paste
cycle.text: Open a terminal, make an empty folder, and type every line above by hand. Run git status after EVERY command, not just where shown -- watching it change is how the three areas actually click.
cycle.hint: git status is the single most-run Git command by experienced developers. If you're ever unsure what state you're in, that's the answer, every time.

cycle.title: Apply it to your own data
cycle.text: Create a real small project folder (even just 2-3 files), git init it, and make three separate commits, each with a real, specific commit message describing what changed.

cycle.title: Reflect & note
cycle.text: What surprised you about staging? Did you expect commit to just save everything automatically?
cycle.placeholder: e.g. I didn't realise a modified-but-unstaged file doesn't get committed at all -- I ran git commit and my change wasn't in the snapshot, which confused me until I checked git status...

cycle.title: Tick off before moving on
checklist: I can explain the three areas (working/staging/repo) in one sentence each.
I ran git init, git add, and git commit myself on a real folder.
I ran git status enough times to see it change between each command.
I made 3 real commits with specific, descriptive messages.
I wrote a reflection note above.
